client: I've been really stressed about things at home lately, and I guess that's why I finally decided to come in. My partner has been telling me they feel like I'm pulling away from them, and honestly, I don't know how to explain that I'm not doing it on purpose — work has just been consuming everything. I'm not even sure talking about it here is going to change anything, but I figured I had to try something before things get worse.
therapist: It takes real courage to show up even when you're not sure it will help, and I'm glad you decided to try. It sounds like you're caught in a really exhausting place — work is draining you, and then you're coming home without much left to give, which is creating distance you never intended. I'm curious, when you imagine your partner seeing that you're *not* pulling away intentionally, what do you most wish they could understand about what your days have been feeling like?

client: I guess... I wish they could understand that by the time I get home, I'm just completely hollowed out. It's not that I don't want to be present with them — it's more like I've spent every last bit of myself trying to hold things together at work, managing everyone else's stress and expectations, and there's genuinely nothing left. And then I feel so guilty about that, which somehow makes it even harder to connect, like I'm already apologizing in my head before I even walk through the door.
therapist: That image of feeling "hollowed out" before you even walk through the door is so vivid, and it makes complete sense that carrying that guilt on top of the exhaustion would make connection feel even harder to reach for. It's like you're already in a kind of emotional debt before the evening even starts, bracing for a conversation you haven't had yet. I'm wondering — when you notice that apologizing-in-your-head feeling on the way home, what does that inner voice actually say to you?

client: It's usually something like "you let them down again" or "you were supposed to be present tonight and you failed." Sometimes it gets more specific, like replaying a moment from the day where I snapped at someone or zoned out in a meeting, and the voice just keeps saying "see, this is who you are now." It's exhausting because by the time I actually get home, I've already convicted myself of something before my partner even has a chance to say a word.
therapist: That phrase — "this is who you are now" — is such a heavy thing to carry, and I want to gently name it as what it is: a thought, not a fact, even though it feels incredibly convincing in those moments. You're essentially putting yourself on trial with no defense attorney, using your most depleted moments as the only evidence of your character. I'm curious — if a close friend described their day to you the way you just described yours, would you look at them and conclude "this is who they are now"?

client: I mean... no, I wouldn't say that to a friend. I'd probably tell them they were just having a rough patch and that it doesn't define them. But it feels different when it's me — like the rules just don't apply the same way, and I can't figure out why I can extend that kindness to everyone else but not to myself.
therapist: What you just noticed is really significant — you already *have* the capacity for compassion, you just haven't been turning it toward yourself, and recognizing that gap is actually the first step to changing it. It's incredibly common for people who are natural caregivers and "holders" of others' stress to develop this double standard, where everyone else deserves grace but they must be held to a harsher account. I'm wondering, what do you think that inner critic is trying to protect you from — is there a part of you that believes being hard on yourself is somehow keeping things from getting worse?

client: I think... yeah, maybe there's something to that. Like if I stop being hard on myself about the loneliness, about not reaching out more to people, then I'll just sink further into it and stop trying altogether. It's almost like the guilt and the self-criticism feel like they're the only thing keeping me from completely giving up on having real connections.
therapist: That's such an honest and insightful thing to recognize — your inner critic has actually been trying to *help* you, acting like a alarm system that keeps you from drifting too far. But I want to gently offer another possibility: what if that constant self-criticism is actually part of what's making connection feel so exhausting and out of reach, rather than pulling you toward it? I'm curious — when the guilt and self-criticism are loudest, do you find yourself actually reaching out more, or does it tend to make you withdraw further?

client: Honestly, when the guilt is loudest I definitely pull back more — like I convince myself that I'd just be a burden to anyone I reached out to, so what's the point. But I'm not sure I fully buy that the self-criticism is the main problem, because it feels like if I just let it go, I'd have nothing pushing me to be better or to even try. It's like you're asking me to remove the one thing that feels like it's keeping me accountable, even if it's uncomfortable.
therapist: That hesitation makes complete sense, and I don't want you to just take my word for it — your skepticism is actually really healthy here. But I'd invite you to notice what you just told me: when the guilt is loudest, you pull back and convince yourself you'd be a burden, which means the very thing you're relying on to keep you connected is actually pushing people away. What if accountability didn't have to feel like punishment — what might it look like to motivate yourself toward connection from a place of "I deserve this" rather than "I owe this"?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but honestly the idea of thinking "I deserve connection" feels almost... arrogant? Like, who am I to just assume people want me around without me earning it somehow. It's easier to understand intellectually than to actually feel it.
therapist: The fact that simply believing you're worthy of connection feels *arrogant* to you is really worth sitting with — it suggests somewhere along the way you learned that your place in relationships had to be constantly earned and justified, rather than simply being a given. That's not a character flaw, it's a belief that was probably taught to you, even if no one said it out loud. I'm curious — can you think of anyone in your life, maybe from earlier on, where you first got the message that belonging was something you had to work for rather than something you simply had?

client: Yeah... I mean, when you put it that way, my dad comes to mind pretty quickly. He wasn't cruel or anything, but praise was rare, and it always felt like it came with conditions — like I had to do something impressive first, and even then it might not come. I guess I just assumed that was normal, that everyone had to prove themselves to be worth someone's time.
therapist: What you just connected is really meaningful — that little kid who learned to earn approval from his dad is still showing up every evening, standing outside your own front door, convinced he has to prove himself before he's allowed to feel at home. And of course that felt normal, because it was *your* normal, but it's worth gently questioning whether your partner is actually asking you to earn your place, or whether that's a very old lens you're still seeing through. I'm wondering — when you think about how your partner actually treats you, do they give you signs that your belonging with them is conditional, or is that more the story your dad's voice is still telling you?

client: Honestly, when I actually stop and think about it... my partner doesn't really do the things my dad did. They don't withhold affection when I mess up, they don't give me the silent treatment or make me feel like I have to perform to be loved. But it's like even knowing that doesn't fully turn off the feeling — I still walk in the door bracing myself, waiting for the moment they'll finally see I'm not enough.
therapist: What you just did is really important — you examined the evidence and found that your partner is actually showing up differently than your dad did, which means that bracing, waiting feeling is your nervous system running an old program that hasn't been updated yet, not an accurate read of your present relationship. That gap between what you *know* and what you *feel* is completely normal, and it's actually where a lot of the real work happens — the head can update quickly, but the body and heart need more time and different kinds of experiences to catch up. I'm curious — has there ever been a moment with your partner, even a small one, where you let your guard down a little and found that the thing you were bracing for didn't actually happen?

client: Yeah, actually... there was this one time a few weeks ago when I was really stressed about work and I just kind of broke down a little in front of him. I was fully expecting him to get uncomfortable and pull away or make some dismissive comment like my dad always would, but he just... sat with me. He didn't try to fix it or leave the room, he just stayed there. I remember feeling almost confused by it, like I kept waiting for the other shoe to drop, and it never did.
therapist: That moment sounds genuinely precious — and the fact that you felt *confused* by his kindness rather than simply comforted by it tells you so much about how deep that old expectation runs. But your partner gave you something really important that night: real evidence, from your own life, that you can be vulnerable and imperfect and still be stayed with. I'm wondering — what would it mean for you to let that moment count, to treat it as just as true and real as all the times your inner critic says you're not enough?
